title: Dietary Fibre: Types, Benefits, Daily Intake and High-Fibre Foods (Indian Guide)
excerpt: Fibre is the nutrient everyone agrees is good and almost nobody eats enough of. This guide explains what dietary fibre is, the two types and what each one does, how much you really need, which foods are richest in fibre (including oats, dals, millets and fruit), what happens if you eat too much, and when fibre supplements make sense. Written by clinical gut health nutritionist Meenu Balaji, with practical Indian food swaps and the evidence behind each claim.

contentHtml:
Fibre is the only nutrient that gets praised at every health talk and ignored at every dinner table. In the US, only about 5% of people reach the recommended intake [1], and in Europe average intakes also sit below recommendations [2].

This guide covers what dietary fibre is, the two types, the benefits that are actually backed by research, how much you need each day, the best high-fibre foods, and what to do if fibre makes you bloated.

What Is Dietary Fibre?

Dietary fibre is the part of plant foods that our own digestive enzymes cannot break down, so it travels on to the large intestine [3]. It is a carbohydrate, but unlike sugar and starch, we absorb very little energy from it. What it does instead is shape stool, slow digestion and feed gut bacteria [4] [5].

Two Types of Dietary Fibre: Soluble vs Insoluble

Most plant foods contain both, in different ratios, and they do different jobs [5] [6].

Soluble fibreInsoluble fibreResistant starch
What it doesDissolves in water into a gel; slows digestion; fermented by gut bacteriaAdds bulk and speeds movement through the gutEscapes digestion and is fermented in the colon
Helps withCholesterol, blood sugar, satiety, microbiomeRegular stoolsMicrobiome, blood sugar
Found inOats, barley, dals, beans, apples, guava, flaxseed, chia, psyllium huskWhole wheat, bran, vegetables, skins of fruitCooked and cooled rice and potatoes, green banana, legumes

A quick correction to a common mix-up: it is soluble fibre that forms a gel and slows sugar absorption, while insoluble fibre mainly adds bulk.

Health Benefits of Dietary Fibre

The big picture: a major series of reviews covering 135 million person-years found that people eating the most fibre had roughly 15 to 30% lower rates of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, colorectal cancer and early death than those eating the least [7], and an umbrella review of meta-analyses points the same way [8].

Here is how it works, system by system.

1. Feeds your gut microbiome

Gut bacteria ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate, which nourish the gut lining and calm the immune system [9] [10]. In mice, a low-fibre diet caused a loss of microbial diversity that deepened over generations [11], and fibre-starved gut bacteria began eating away the protective mucus layer [12].

Fibre-derived fatty acids also eased allergic airway inflammation in mice, one more hint of how far gut bacteria reach [13]. For the bigger picture, read my posts on prebiotics and probiotics and the top 10 foods for gut health.

2. Protects your heart and lowers cholesterol

In one meta-analysis, every extra 7 g of fibre a day was linked with about a 9% lower risk of cardiovascular disease [14] and a lower risk of first stroke [15], and a large US cohort showed the same pattern [16]. Gel-forming soluble fibre binds bile acids, so the liver pulls more cholesterol from the blood.

About 3 g a day of oat beta-glucan lowered LDL cholesterol by roughly 0.25 mmol/L [17], and a daily serving of pulses lowered LDL modestly too [18]. Higher fibre intake is also linked with lower C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation [19]. Related reading: how to reduce cholesterol naturally and which fats are bad for cholesterol.

3. Steadies blood sugar

Soluble fibre slows the release of sugar after a meal. Higher fibre intake was linked with a lower risk of type 2 diabetes [20], and fibre supplementation improved blood sugar control in people who already had it [21]. In a clinical study, a high-fibre diet that boosted certain acid-producing gut bacteria improved HbA1c in people with type 2 diabetes [22]. See how to lower blood sugar naturally or my diabetes nutrition service.

4. Supports a healthy weight

Fibre, especially the thick, gel-forming kind, tends to make meals more filling, though results on body weight vary between trials [23] [24]. During calorie-restricted diets, higher fibre intake predicted greater weight loss and better adherence [25], and over ten years young adults with higher fibre intakes gained less weight [26]. Fibre helps; it is not a magic wand. Juicing removes most of it, which is why I prefer whole fruit (see ABC juice).

5. Protects the colon

Every extra 10 g of fibre a day was linked with about a 10% lower risk of colorectal cancer [27], and a European cohort found about a quarter lower risk in the highest-fibre group [28]. Higher intakes are also linked with a lower risk of diverticular disease [29], although one colonoscopy study found no link between a low-fibre diet and diverticulosis itself, so the evidence is not as clear-cut as often claimed [30].

6. Eases piles (haemorrhoids)

Fibre reduced persistent symptoms and bleeding in people with haemorrhoids [31], because softer stools mean less straining, one of the main drivers of the problem [32]. Any rectal bleeding still needs a doctor to rule out other causes.

7. Helps constipation, but not always

In constipation, extra fibre increased stool frequency [33]. But in a small study of people with chronic constipation, cutting fibre down improved bowel frequency and reduced bloating [34], and specialists have long warned that fibre is not a cure-all, especially in slow-transit constipation [35]. I explain why in functional constipation: why “eat more fibre” doesn’t always work, why am I always constipated and how to relieve constipation fast.

8. IBS: the type of fibre matters

In irritable bowel syndrome, soluble fibre such as ispaghula helped, while insoluble bran did not and could worsen symptoms [36] [37]. Some fibres are also high in fermentable carbohydrates, and a low FODMAP diet reduced IBS symptoms in a randomised trial [38]. More in stomach pain after every meal, foods to avoid with IBS and SIBO diet foods.

Clinical insight: Fibre is not one nutrient. Matching the type of fibre to the symptom (soluble for loose or IBS-type stools, plenty of fluid and gradual increases for sluggish bowels) matters more than hitting a number on the label.

How Much Dietary Fibre Do You Need? (Recommended and Daily Intake)

GroupTypical target
Adults, WHO and UK-style guidanceAt least 25 g a day; the UK advises 30 g [2] [7]
Adults, USAbout 14 g per 1,000 kcal, roughly 25 g for women and 38 g for men [4]
ChildrenA common rule is age plus 5 g a day [39]

The same review that set these targets noted that higher intakes may protect even more, so treat 25 to 30 g as a floor, not a ceiling [7].

Resistant starch:

Resistant starch escapes digestion in the small intestine. They are used by the beneficial bacteria in the large intestine.

Food Sources of Dietary Fiber:

  • Cellulose is present in good amounts in cereals and vegetables.
  • Fruits with edible seeds like strawberries, carrots and other root vegetables have high amounts of lignin.
  • Whole-grain cereals and bran are rich in hemicellulose.
  • Fruits like apples, bananas, and guava contain pectin.
  • Oats and flaxseed are good sources of soluble fiber.

Change in food habits:

Research studies of the Palaeolithic (old stone age) period indicate that about 65 per cent of the food consumed was uncultivated fruits and vegetables, which were high in dietary fiber (12.6 g/100 g).

They also consumed game meat, which had more unsaturated fatty acids, protein and fewer calories and provided more micronutrients than our current diet (Susan Sungsoo, 2001). This helped them lead a very healthy lifestyle.

We, on the other hand, are more inclined to eat processed and ultra-processed foods for convenience.

These processed foods hardly contain any fiber and have added additives to increase shelf-life. Our present-day diet is energy dense and nutrient scarce, leading to several health conditions.

Many food brands claim to contain a sufficient amount of fiber in the product. Read the nutrition label to see how much it actually provides and what the source is. If it is highly processed, then you may not benefit from the fiber.

Food Rich in Dietary Fibre: High-Fibre Foods List

The table shows approximate fibre per 100 g. Values vary between databases and brands, so treat them as a guide.

Guava5 gSoluble (pectin)

Apple (with skin)2.5 gSoluble (pectin)

Dietary fibre in oats. Oats give about 10 g of fibre per 100 g dry, so a 40 g bowl provides roughly 4 g. Their beta-glucan lowers LDL cholesterol [17] and blunts the blood sugar rise after a meal [40]. Pick plain rolled or steel-cut oats, not sugary instant sachets.

Dals, beans and chickpeas. The most budget-friendly fibre in the Indian kitchen. Pulses improved cholesterol [18] and blood sugar control [41]. Try my easy lentil recipes.

Seeds, millets and whole grains. Add chia seeds (see the chia pudding recipes), flaxseed, ragi, bajra, brown or wild rice, jackfruit flour roti and sprouted buckwheat.

Resistant starch. Rice and potatoes that are cooked and then cooled contain more resistant starch [42], and cooling cooked white rice raised its resistant starch and lowered the glycaemic response in one study [43]. Curd rice, anyone?

Watch the label: many “high-fibre” biscuits and bars get their fibre from added isolated fibres, not whole foods. Check the ingredient list.

Can You Eat Too Much Dietary Fibre?

Yes, or at least too much too fast. Jumping from 10 g to 40 g in a week can cause gas, bloating, cramps and, with too little water, even harder stools. Increase by a few grams every week or so, drink enough fluid, and spread fibre across meals. If bloating persists, see how to get rid of bloating. Very bran-heavy diets can also crowd out other foods, so keep variety.

Be extra careful if you have IBS, SIBO, a bowel narrowing or an inflammatory bowel condition: the right fibre type and amount can differ, and guidelines advise individualising fibre in people with strictures [44]. Very low-carbohydrate diets can also leave fibre short, as I discuss in keto and gut health.

Fibre Supplements: Psyllium and Others

Supplements can fill a gap but are not a substitute for food. Psyllium husk (isabgol) lowered LDL cholesterol in a meta-analysis of trials [45] and improved blood sugar control [46], and it changed the gut microbiota in a small study of constipated people [47].

Still, a high-fibre diet lowered C-reactive protein while a fibre supplement did not [48], which is one reason I put food first. If you use one, start low, take it with plenty of water, separate it from medicines and check with your doctor. See also how to choose the best probiotics.

Fibre for Teens and Athletes

Growing teens need enough fibre for regular digestion, and the age plus 5 g rule is a handy start [39]. Athletes face another issue: hard exercise itself can upset the gut [49], and the gut can be trained to tolerate fuel and fibre [50]. In practice, most athletes eat plenty of fibre in training and trim it in the hours before a race. Get a plan from my sports nutrition or child and teen nutrition service.

How to Get More Dietary Fibre Every Day

  1. Swap refined grains for oats, millets, brown rice or whole-wheat atta.
  2. Add a fruit or vegetable to breakfast, and eat fruit whole with the skin where safe.
  3. Put dals, rajma or chana on the plate daily.
  4. Sprinkle chia or ground flaxseed on curd, porridge or smoothies.
  5. Snack on guava, apple, carrot or roasted chana instead of biscuits.
  6. Increase slowly and drink water.

Dietary Fibre FAQs

  1. What are the two types of dietary fibre?

Soluble fibre dissolves into a gel and slows digestion; insoluble fibre adds bulk and helps stool move along [6].

  1. How much dietary fibre should I eat per day?

Aim for at least 25 to 30 g a day as an adult [7].

  1. Which foods have the most fibre?

Chia, flaxseed, almonds, oats, pulses and guava are among the richest, as the table above shows.

  1. Are oats high in fibre?

Yes, about 10 g per 100 g dry, and the beta-glucan helps cholesterol [17].

  1. Can too much fibre be bad?

Too much, too quickly can cause bloating and cramps, and some conditions need a tailored approach [34] [44].

  1. Does fibre help with piles?

It can reduce symptoms and bleeding by keeping stools soft [31]. Bleeding should always be checked by a doctor.

  1. Is a fibre supplement as good as food?

Not quite. Supplements help in specific situations, but whole foods bring more than fibre alone [48].

  1. Does fibre help weight loss?

It supports fullness and diet adherence, but it works best alongside overall diet quality [25].

Work With a Gut Health Nutritionist

If fibre leaves you bloated, constipated or confused, the answer is rarely “eat more” or “eat less”, it is working out which fibre, how much and when for your gut. Explore my gut health nutrition service or contact me.

This article is educational and does not replace medical advice. See a doctor for rectal bleeding, persistent bowel changes or unexplained weight loss.
